newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore opposition seeks to boost poll chances.
newsitem.headline: Singapore opposition seeks to boost poll chances.

text.p: In a move to boost their election chances, Singapore's seven opposition parties have agreed to avoid three-cornered fights in all but three constituencies they will contest.

J.B. Jeyaretnam, secretary-general of the Worker's Party, told Reuters on Wednesday the opposition aimed to clinch at least 10 of the 83 seats to be contested in elections due by April. They now have four.
Many analysts expect the government to call elections in late December or early January.
Jeyaretnam said the opposition planned to contest up to 40 seats with his party seeking to field 12 to 16 candidates.
"People want to have an effective opposition and we believe this can happen," Jeyaretnam said.
He said he expected the ruling People's Action Party's (PAP) share of the votes to dip to at least 55 percent from just over 60 percent in the 1991 election.
Jeyaratnam noted that even Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong has said the PAP focus now was to win as many seats as possible rather than on the share of votes.
Jeyaretnam chaired a meeting of opposition party leaders late on Tuesday to agree on how to avoid splitting the opposition vote.
He said that since the deal excluded independent candidates, there could still be three-cornered fights where independents decided to run.
The three areas in dispute include single and multi-member group representation constituencies (GRC) where candidates stand as a slate, he said.
"There is a quite a pleasant atmosphere among the opposition parties and I believe we could resolve the differences through informal meetings," Jeyaretnam said.

Chee Soon Juan, secretary-general of the Singapore Democratic Party agreed. "As long as the opposition understands that their main political opponent is the PAP it's a good start," he said. "Subsequently, there could be more work for them to cooperate further but that would take time. When the time comes, the party leaders would be able to get together."

The 70-year-old Jeyaretnam won a by-election in 1981, the first opposition seat since independence in 1965. But he was disqualified from holding office for five years in 1986 after being convicted on charges of making false statements about his party's accounts.
He won an appeal in London's Privy Council but his petition for a presidential pardon was rejected.
Jeyaretnam said the opposition planned to contest up to 40 with his party seeking to field 12 to 16 candidates.
